# AKSHA — Evaluation

*Generated by `scripts/eval_final.py` at commit `674fdca13169de9ae2de0cb70a02fad96490d177`,
against triage-service revision `triage-service-00006-gnw`. Full machine-readable
numbers: `eval/outputs/final_report.json` (gitignored, regenerable — see that
script's docstring). Read time: under 2 minutes.*

## What this is not claiming

Three things, stated before any number below, because a benchmark result is only
as good as what it doesn't hide:

**1. This is measured on ESA-ADB's Mission2 dataset, not OPSSAT-AD.** The
detector, gate calibration, and golden set are built on ESA-ADB's **Mission2**
benchmark: a different spacecraft, 22 features, an hourly-window adapter with
its own train/calibration/test split (137,235 / 23,970 / 168,410 windows), and
none of it touches `data/dataset.csv` or `data/segments.csv` (the files
`scripts/fetch_data.py` downloads). This is the build dataset per
[ADR-015](adr/ADR-015.md), which supersedes `ADR-006`'s original OPSSAT-AD
choice; PRD and README are updated to match. Restated here because it changes
what every metric below means, not because it's unresolved.

**2. No anomaly-only detection metric is reported on the test split.** Mission2's
test split contains exactly **4 anomaly-labelled windows**, all from a single
annotated event on 2001-12-14 touching three channels. Four positives from one
event cannot support precision, recall, F1, or MCC as a meaningful number —
`docs/mission2-adapter-notes.md` states this plainly, and ESA-ADB's own paper
hits the identical wall on the full Mission2 channel set (arXiv 2406.17826:
no algorithm identified the actual anomalies "in this overabundance of rare
nominal events"). The 7 benchmark-style metrics below are reported with
`rare_event ∪ anomaly` as the positive class instead — 5,650 positives, real
support — which is ESA-ADB's own pooling convention for the same reason
(arXiv 2406.17826, Table 2: *"there are no algorithms... that can explicitly
distinguish between anomalies and rare nominal events"*). Point-adjusted F1 is
not reported anywhere in this document (CLAUDE.md).

**3. The recognition distance separates fault from expected operation, but not
cleanly — AUC ≈ 0.79–0.80, not ≈ 1.0.** That is the honest ceiling. It is why
the gate is three-way (`confirm` / `disputed` / `reject`) rather than a binary
cut: `disputed` exists because roughly a fifth of the operating point's
neighbourhood genuinely does not decide from this signal alone. See
*Separability* below for the exact number, freshly measured, against the 0.788
figure recorded as a code comment when the band was chosen.

## 1. Detector performance

`aksha_core/artifacts/mission2_iforest.joblib` (`iforest-conformal-0.1.0`), scored
live this session against the Mission2 test split (168,410 windows), epsilon
0.01 (99th-percentile conformal threshold).

**7 benchmark-style metrics**, positive class `rare_event ∪ anomaly` (n=5,650 of
168,410; see disclosure #2 above for why anomaly-only is not reported):

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.979 |
| Precision | 0.704 |
| Recall | 0.650 |
| F1 | 0.676 |
| MCC | 0.666 |
| AUC-ROC | 0.853 |
| AUC-PR | 0.653 |

Point-adjusted F1: not computed (CLAUDE.md — known to overstate performance on
this task class; not reported even as a secondary number here, since it adds
nothing beyond the above).

Anomaly-only, unscored, for transparency: 2 of 4 flagged (50%).

**Score separation by true category** (test split, detector's raw decision score):

| Category | n | Mean score | Above threshold |
|---|---|---|---|
| nominal | 162,760 | −0.150 | 0.9% |
| rare_event | 5,646 | +0.009 | 65.1% |
| anomaly | 4 | +0.008 | 50.0% |

Cross-checked live against the committed `mission2_iforest_train_report.json`
— identical to 6 decimal places, confirming the artifact and test split are
unchanged since training.

## 2. Separability of the recognition distance

The gate decides on distance-to-nearest-rare_event-exemplar, not the detector's
score. Recomputed live this session (`scripts/calibrate_recognition.py:nearest_rare_distances`,
train period, 144,397 scored windows — no new modeling, the same metric the gate
uses in production):

| Comparison | AUC (measured live) | Prior comment (code) |
|---|---|---|
| anomaly vs. (nominal ∪ rare_event) — "fault vs. expected" | **0.795** | 0.788 (`calibrate_recognition.py:58`) |
| anomaly vs. rare_event only | **0.610** | 0.593 (`workflow.py:174`) |

Both drifted up by ~1–2 points from the code comments' figures. Neither
comment's number was ever written back into the calibration artifact (its
`separability_auc` field was `null` until this run) — small drift, consistent
direction, not investigated further here.

## 3. Gate vs. LLM vs. naive baseline — 200 held-out faults

`build_context_reference.py` reserves 200 anomaly windows out of the train
period specifically so fault sensitivity can be measured on windows the
verifier has never retrieved (`HOLDOUT_ANOMALIES = 200`). Re-run live this
session (STEP 5) against the current code (post-#16) and current calibration
— not read from any prior report, because we just learned this service went
33 hours running pre-#12 code without anyone knowing (see the deploy
post-mortem this session).

| | Confirm rate | n |
|---|---|---|
| **Gate** (deterministic, decides the outcome) | **88.5%** (177/200) | 200 |
| LLM alone (audit only, does not decide) | 51.5% (103/200) | 200 |
| Naive "always confirm" baseline | 100% | 200 |

The naive baseline is trivially 100% because this holdout is anomaly-only by
construction — it is not a competing detector, it is the ceiling this one
metric can't rule out by itself. The gate's real contribution is specificity on
*non*-fault windows, which this all-positive set can't measure — see the golden
set (§4) and the calibration's ambiguous-band table for that half of the story.

**Drift check against prior claims:**

| Source | Gate | LLM | n |
|---|---|---|---|
| **This run (live, post-#16)** | **88.5%** | **51.5%** | 200 |
| Task message (this session) | 88% | 52% | — |
| `workflow.py:170-176` code comment (as it read before this session) | 93% | 70% | 100 |

The task message's figures match this run almost exactly. The **code comment
was the stale one** — it predated whatever last changed the calibration or
prompt, and had never been updated. Fixed in the same session: `workflow.py`'s
comment now cites this run's 88.5%/51.5%/AUC 0.610 directly, so it no longer
drifts from what's actually measured.

## 4. Golden set — 22 fixed windows

`tests/fixtures/golden_set.json`, scored live this session. Calibration
unchanged since the golden set was built (gate threshold 2.0658, band
[1.3428, 2.7888] — confirmed identical, both then and now).

| Group | n | Expected | Matched |
|---|---|---|---|
| clear_fault | 4 | confirm | 4/4 |
| clear_expected | 7 | reject | 7/7 |
| clear_nominal | 7 | reject | 7/7 |
| ambiguous | 4 | *(none — no expected verdict by design)* | all 4 → `disputed` |

**Scored agreement (ambiguous excluded): 18/18 (100%).**

## 5. Live confirmation — the audit column doing its job

Real end-to-end run today through `triage-service-00006-gnw` (the redeployed,
numpy-fixed revision): published via `scripts/publish_stub.py --window anomaly`
→ `telemetry-in` → detector-service (score +0.103, conformal_p 0.00063,
flagged) → triage-service → Firestore `incidents/frag-anomaly-1787527553`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Gate distance | 1.4131 |
| Threshold / band | 2.0658 / [1.3428, 2.7888] |
| Gate verdict | `disputed` |
| LLM verdict | `confirm` |
| Final verdict | `disputed` (gate's, not the model's) |
| Routed to | `log` (Advisory) |
| Slack delivery | `delivered` — confirmed 2xx from the real `slack-log` webhook |

The LLM read this as a genuine fault; the gate placed the calibrated distance
inside the uncertainty band and returned `disputed`; `disputed` is what routed.
The model's read never touched the outcome — exactly the design in
`workflow.py:168`, *"the gate decides, alone."*
